items.body: Mount Analogue is a landmark work from a master artist in tribute to the great chain of influence that goes from one seeker to another, from one artist to another. I consider it another essential clue in my own quest for discovering an applying obscure knowledge. Climbing the symbolic peaks of René Daumal‘s unfinished Mountain Mount Analogue by Bill Laswell + P.St (featuring N.P. Molvaer, H. Kaiser, P. Howard, G. Haynes, P. Apfelbaum…)   I remember the first time I bought music by Bill Laswell. It was 1998, my last year of high school, and I was in Cleveland with a friend on a spring break road trip fueled by punk rock shows and NoDoz. Record stores were an important part of that trip too, and I remember finding a section of CD’s marked “Bill Laswell” and I was intrigued. I picked up a CD called Jihad (Points of Order) by one of his voluminous side projects, Automaton. It consisted of two long tracks, each around 23 minutes. The album featured musician Tetsu Inoue whose name didn’t mean anything to me then, though now it occupies a special place in my long-term love affair with ambient music. It also featured Lili Haydn on violin, and Nicky Skopelitis, a frequent collaborator with Laswell, on guitar. In my opinion, Skopelitis could get a lot more love for his expressive guitar work then I’ve seen. Of course, Bill Laswell was also on the record providing bass, electronics, treatments, and without question, his expansive musical vision. It was the beginning of a journey into his wide-ranging musical world. I started keeping my eyes and ears open for anything Laswell had his hand in, and as I would soon find out, his hand was in all kinds of interesting material; and Material happened to be the next group of his I discovered. The next real gateway drug, however, was the double album under the Axiom Ambient moniker, Lost in Translation. With song titles like “Cosmic Trigger” how could one go wrong in picking up an album like this unheard? It was around the same time I was reading deeply across the works of Robert Anton Wilson, and his book Cosmic Trigger had set me off on my own quest for Sirius. There is also a song on that record called “Holy Mountain” which brings us to the present album, Mount Analogue, marking yet another vast peak in Laswell’s long career. There is a connection between that song and this album. This musical journey pays tribute to René Daumal and his enchanting world of mysteries and magic. The album shares its title with Daumal’s novel, Mount Analogue: A Novel of Symbolically Authentic Non-Euclidean Adventures in Mountain Climbing, published posthumously in 1952, eight years after the author’s untimely death. Another connection that encompasses Laswell’s singular talent as a sound sculptor and practitioner of the alchemy of music reconstruction and mix translation, as well as his ability as a studio conductor in bringing the work of disparate musicians into progressive harmony. Lost in Translation featured a vast army of adventurous ambient musicians whose work he fused into its singular form. Inou and Skopelitis both made contributions, as did Terre Thaemlitz, The Orb, and various players from the expanded funakdelic pantheon. The cast of supporting musicians on Mount Analogue is a little bit less than Lost in Translation, but still substantial, and reflects another wave of audio connection and total immersion in contemporary music. Contributors to this poetic musical vision include Bill Laswell (bass), Henry Kaiser (guitar), Anna Clementi (vocals), Percy Howard (voice), Hideo Yamaki (percussion), Graham Haynes (cornet), Dorian Cheah (violin), Nils Petter Molvaer (trumpet), Peter Apfelbaum (keyboard), and P.ST (concept, electronics), who all lend their talents to a series of excerpts from Daumal‘s text. Beyond P.ST, who I’ve written about before, I’m not familiar with the work of these musicians. That in itself is an invitation to discover their other work, expanding the field of musical knowledge and mystico-musical kinship. Finding a CD in a record shop has the possibility of sending a person out on a quest. The references to books and novels, the different artists, all become keys for future exploration when trying to find a way through labyrinthine tunnels of reality. “And what about you? What are you looking for?” Daumal asks. Me? I was looking for the kind of clues Laswell leaves for fellow seekers. Directions for navigating my path out of the labyrinth and up into the foothills towards the ascent beyond. Mount Analogue by Bill Laswell + P.St (featuring N.P. Molvaer, H. Kaiser, P. Howard, G. Haynes, P. Apfelbaum…)   HOLY MOUNTAINS :: Another linking thread is how the song “Holy Mountain” from Lost in Translation, and the first fifty minute piece “Mount Analogue” both deal with the alchemy of ascent. There are many kinds of land formations that humanity looks to for spiritual connection. The forests with their groves of ancient trees and ages of wisdom. The desert with its dry heat and ability to conjure visionary vistas. Rivers without end whose meandering flow bridges the material and immaterial, offering purification and pilgrimage to those who attend their rites. And the mountains, the holy mountains, the high places of the world. All across the world mountains are revered. According to Shinto beliefs Mount Fuji in Japan is the dwelling place of the spirits and deities. Two other holy mountains in Japan complete a trinity of such, Mount Haku and Mount Tate. Mount Kailash in the Ngari Prefecture of Tibet, China is considered the spiritual center of the universe in Hinduism, home to Shiva and Parvati. For Buddhists that same mountain is known as Mount Meru and the place where the deity Chakrasamvara dwells. It is also revered by Jains and in the Tibetan Bon religion, and is considered the place where the first Jain Tirthankara (a kind of savior) achieved liberation and freedom from the wheel of birth and rebirth. In the Bible, Moses had to go up Mount Sinai to receive the Ten Commandments. Yet another link is to the 1973 surrealist mindfuck film Holy Mountain by Alejandro Jodorowsky. The Chilean filmmaker was inspired by René Daumal’s novel Mount Analogue, a book that has held several generations of creators and makers under its spell. The second epic tracks here is “Jodorowsky’s Peradam.” We will get to that, but I want to explore some other correspondences that float into my mind when I listen to this fresh masterpiece. Another person who fell under the spell of Daumal was John Zorn. He has his own album called Mount Analogue as well, out on his Tzadik label in 2012. Zorn is another master at bringing disparate musicians together for magical exegesis of sound. Zorn and Laswell are likewise frequent collaborators with each other. The two have worked on numerous projects including in the band Painkiller. In 2021 they recorded a record together called The Cleansing for Tzadik featuring six songs. The first five songs on that album are dedicated to various mystical, magical and artistic luminaries who have inspired the composers. Included on that record is a song “Alejandro Jodorowsky.” All of this makes sense when you consider that Laswell and Zorn have been friends since the 1970s. That they share similar obsessions and influences should come as no surprise to those who’ve been following along. As Laswell wrote in an interview for the Music Hertz blog, “We have different approaches, but knowing each other for so long has shaped our tastes. While we may have different approaches to music, there is no denying the significant impact of John‘s work on my tastes and creative outlook. On the other hand, you can say he didn’t influence me at all. We just have a great relationship. Our collaborations have been characterized by a sense of mutual respect and a shared commitment to artistic integrity. We understand that the strength of our partnership lies in our differences, and we cherish the creative energy that emerges from our diverse perspectives.” The energy presented on Laswell’s Mount Analogue is of a different point of order than Zorn’s. But they can all be enjoyed together, along with Daumal’s novel, and Jodorwosky’s film. All of this forms a rich creative and nourishing creative stew. Yet Daumal’s novel is short, and it was left unfinished when he died at age 36. Why has this little short novel been so important to so many people? How did it come to be, and how did it come to influence the living masters of Jodorowsky, Zorn and Laswell in the creation of their own epic works? The answer gets into the heart of the mysticism and magic that wind their worth through the creative artifacts manifested by all of these artists. To get to there, we have to take brief detour into the mysterious world G. I. Gurdjieff, a master musician in his own right, and his circle of disciples. Exploring the history of ideas around all this material is very much a huge part of my own enjoyment of the music. However if you want to skip reading these origin stories about Gurdjieff, his friend Alexander de Salzmann who formed a massive influence René Daumal and became a character his novel, you can scroll down to the sections Mount Analogue and Jodrowsky’s Peradam, where I finally talk about the music itself. Mount Analogue by Bill Laswell + P.St (featuring N.P. Molvaer, H. Kaiser, P. Howard, G. Haynes, P. Apfelbaum…)   CIRCLES OF MYSTIC ART :: Zorn’s entire catalog is replete with hermetic, Kabbalistic, mystical and magic iconography, as is Laswell’s. They name drop names and hints in the form of album art with strange symbols and sigils alluding to mysterious figures who have influenced history from the fringes of culture. For those who are in the know, they are in the know. For those who aren’t, curiosity gets piqued, and the quest begins. John Zorn’s album draws inspiration “from the life and work of the towering spiritual figure Georges Ivanovitch Gurdjieff.” The brief liner notes and catalog description doen’t even mention Daumal. Yet Daumal’s book was influenced by his friendship with Alexander de Salzmann, a pupil of Gurdjieff. So why did Gurdjieff have pupils? He wasn’t teaching grade school, but was a teacher of spiritual matters. Hailing from Alexandropol, Yerevan Governorate, Russian Empire (now Gyumri, Armenia) he was of Greek ancestry. As he sought meaning to life went out on a quest in his early adulthood. This quest for wisdom led him to Egypt, Iran, India, Central Asia and Tibet. At the heart of Gurdjieff’s oeuvre was the notion that people aren’t really conscious of themselves and exist in an entranced hypnosis like a waking sleep. Sometimes they wake up for a spell only to fall back in the stupor of slumber, like automatons. Yet having once glimpsed the awakened state, he thought it was possible for people to reach that consciousness again. His search for the means of waking up led him back to ancient truths and wisdom traditions that he thought could help people wake up. It’s my own contention that music made by the likes of Bill Laswell and John Zorn can serve as one of the vehicles for helping people snap out of the trance. Daumal took Gurdjieff’s teaching and put it this way in his novel, “All the means we’ve been given to stay alert we use to ornament our sleep. If instead of endlessly inventing new ways to make life more comfortable we’d apply our ingenuity to fabricating instruments to jog man out of his torpor!” Gurdjieff had seen that torpor in the form of a mass psychosis that had led to the mass slaughter of World War I. He feared that those caught up in the perambulations of a sleepwalker were more susceptible to being controlled by others. (The psychologist Wilhelm Reich would also question the way people voluntarily turned themselves over to one form of authoritarianism after another as explored in his book The Mass Psychology of Fascism. It’s still relevant.) Helping people get out of this trance became Gurdjieff’s life work. Gurdjieff had noted that most people in the past who had wanted to awaken retreated to monasteries, ashrams and hermit caves. This is not really possible for everyone in any society. He also noted that it was usually just one part of a person that got developed in various esoteric schools or sects: their heart, mind or body. He looked for another way, and that way came to be called the “Fourth Way” by his student P.D. Ouspensky who furthered these teachings. The Fourth Way would work on the mind, body and emotions together and in harmony to help bring awakening to individuals. One of those individuals who set out on this path was Daumal’s friend Alexander de Salzmann, from the country Georgia. He was a painter, theater designer and stage lighting artist who counted Wassily Kandinsky and Rainer Maria Rilke as his friends, tapped in to the artistic and spiritual currents of his time. He had been living in Russia but in 1919, because of the revolution, he left with his wife to live in Germany. It wasn’t long after that Gurdjieff and his pupils arrived, and they were introduced by another mutual friend, the Ukranian composer Thomas de Hartmann. The Salzmann’s and Gurdjieff hit it off and they became immediately involved in “the work.” They worked with him as close disciples and collaborators to further it along. After various activities in different countries for several years, Gurdjieff and his followers arrived in France in 1922. It was here that they established his Institute for the Harmonious Development of Man at the Prieuré. The Institute was a place for seekers to live together communally in pursuit of psychic transformation under Gurdjieff who provided both guidance and friction. Conditions were often difficult and hard labor was meted out along with spiritual exercises and practice of art and music. The purpose was to create “conditions in which man could be continually reminded of the sense and aim of his existence by an unavoidable friction between his consciousness and the automatic manifestations of his nature.” Thus begin eight years of intense activity. De Salzmann was painting, his wife was dancing, Gurdjieff went on trip to America and got into a near fatal auto accident. Gurdjieff worked closely with Jeanne de Salzmann in developing movements for her dance, and all of them were trying to keep the Institute running. Yet by 1930 Salzmann had disappeared from the Institute. He felt that Gurdjieff’s attentions to his wife’s dancing were a bit much, while his own considerable talents as a painter had been neglected by his teacher. It seemed to be a bit of a triangle between the master and the married couple. There were rumors that de Salzmann’s son, Michel, might have actually been the son of Gurdjieff, so there may have been something else going on leading to Alexandre’s period of discontent. Whatever the actual case may be, de Salzmann left and joined a monastery, noting that “I had entered … under the name of Brother Petrus. I came out with the title of Father Sogol.” After that he made his living as an antique dealer and interior decorator. Father Sogol was the name given to de Salzmann in Daumal’s singular novel. It was in October of that year that started hanging out at the Café Figon on the Boulevard St. Germain. This was the place where he and the bohemian circle around artist Josef Šíma went to drink after their meetings in Sima’s studio. Daumal, Sima and the others noticed this man, always drinking calvados and writing scripts in Arabic and Chinese. One evening Šíma was struck with recognition for de Salzmann, having previously met him at a publishers event some seven years earlier. He went over to the now familiar man, and introduced the artist to his own circle. De Salzmann later approached them again and after they conversed for some time, asked them to hold their arms out straight to the side for as long as they could, testing them. Some minutes later, Daumal was the only one who still had his arms extended. After this test was completed de Salzmann that he was very taken by the character of Daumal. The two became friends and now the older artist had a younger pupil to transmit the Gurdjieffean gnosis. For Daumal it was a revalation and he became enamored and totally devoted to the work. Mount Analogue by Bill Laswell + P.St (featuring N.P. Molvaer, H. Kaiser, P. Howard, G. Haynes, P. Apfelbaum…)   MOUNT ANALOGUE :: Daumal had already been on his own journey by the time he met de Salzmann. Born in Boulzicourt, Ardennes, France in 1908, by the time he reached his teens he was already known for his precocious avantgarde poetry that was landing him in the leading journals of the time. A literary wunderkind, he came under the spell of Alfred Jarry, who had died the year before he was born. Jarry was a symbolist writer, forerunner of surrealism and Dada, author of the play Ubu Roi, and the novel Exploits and Opinions of Dr. Faustroll, Pataphysician. Daumal came to think of himself as a pataphysician. That is, someone who practices the “science of imaginary solutions,” a philosophical concept created by Jarry. Like other teens, Daumal got interested in the effects of drugs and what they might do to his consciousness. Unlike many other teens, what he messed around with was carbon tetrachloride. This chemical has a direct effect on the central nervous system and in the past was used as a cleaning agent, in early refrigeration systems and fire extinguishers. It was dangerous stuff and got phased out. Daumal wasn’t afraid of a bit of danger, and if taking the drug took him closer to the precipice of death, that was okay with him, because he wanted to see and know what was on the other side. These experiments allowed him to, in his own words, “burst the limits of the possible and projected me brutally into another world.” The lingering after effects of the chemical in his body also might have been one of the contributing factors to his early death at age 36 while he was writing Mount Analogue. He was friends with a group of misfits who were so weird they even got kicked out of the surrealists, which was fine with them because they thought the surrealists and dadaists were too passe. These fellows called themselves Les  Phrères Simplistes or The Simple Brothers, and included the poet and morphine addict Roger Gilbert-Lecomte, the novelist Roger Vailland and another writer Robert Meyrat. They were an inseparable bunch and beyond their shared literary aspirations, they shared a commitment to exploring their consciousness. Bohemians to the core, they were sometimes referred to as “the many headed Rimbaud.”  Together they created the literary journal Le Grand Jeu and put three issues into circulation. The Czech modernist painter Josef Šíma became the artistic director for the publication. It was in the pages of Le Grand Jeu where they denounced surrealism, and in turn had their provisional micro-society in turn denounced by Andre Breton. After Daumal’s encounter with de Salzmann at the Café Figon he increasingly gave himself over to the teachings of Gurdjieff transmitted to him by way of his new friend, and he kept busy writing including a column on pataphysics for La Nouvelle Revue Française. Alexander de Salzmann had already died in 1934, and after his passing, Daumal continued to study and work with his widow Jeananne. She had set up communal homes dedicated to “the Work”, and he worked with her in those settings. By 1938 he was working the work directly with Gurdjieff himself. It was the same year his first novel A Night of Serious Drinking was published. It contains allusions to Gurdjieff’s ideas of being asleep in a dreamlike existence through the metaphor of drunkenness, but it was his second novel, the one he died in midst of writing, that shows the unmistakable influence of Gurdjieff. He started Mount Analogue in 1940. Part of his inspiration was to “do for metaphysics what Jules Verne had done for physics.” Indeed, the book can be looked at as being related to science fiction. It is the record of expedition to climb a mountain that most people in the world do not even know exists, a mountain range that cannot be seen, even though it is the highest mountain range in the world, much higher even than the Himalayas. The books narrator talks about “how it was proved that a hitherto unknown continent really existed, with mountains much higher than the Himalayas; how it happened that no one had detected it before; how we reached it; what creatures we met there; how another expedition, pursuing quite different goals, barely missed destruction; how we have begun little by little to put down roots, so to speak, in this new world; and how, nevertheless, the journey has barely begun.” These are some of the words quoted in Bill Laswell’s masterful musical interpretation of the novel on the first fifty minute side titled after the book. It is a musical work that begins in sections with various spoken quotes from the book. Then he and his fellow musicians come in and explore the meaning of that quote through their instruments. Voice, cornet, and electronic soundscapes drift along a cool breeze in the opening section. Attainment is still far ahead, but there is buoyant joy in beginning the journey. Thin violin lines begin to weave in complex counterpoint with delicate fretwork on bass and guitar. As the music progresses bits start to get processed, glitched, a phrase will skip like a skipping CD snapping the listener out of the trance of sleep and returning them to the present musical moment. Swirls of chaos threaten the first wave of bliss with the panic that comes to any seeker, and from this panic, new ways around temporary obstacles are improvised. Escalating electronic sweeps and swoops climb and rise marking new vistas. A female voice, in keening ululations recalls the female voice on “Holy Mountain” on the Axiom Ambient album, creating a correspondence system of parallel musical symbolism. So it goes on through several movements, each inaugurated by a slowly read quote from the book. Each quote can be heard before sinking into a new phase of discursive meditation along with the music, each section bringing the listener closer to the peak, closer to discovering Mount Analogue itself. Mount Analogue by Bill Laswell + P.St (featuring N.P. Molvaer, H. Kaiser, P. Howard, G. Haynes, P. Apfelbaum…)   JODOROWSKY’S PERADAM :: The second half of the album is dedicated to a series of five intricate solo electric guitar fantasias by Henry Kaiser. The first of these, clocking in at 48 minutes,  is titled “Jodorowsky’s Peradam,” taking us further along the journey. Jodorowsky’s story is as epic as any of the other mystical artists, seekers and musicians already written about whose lives have been touched by the teachings of Gurdjieff. He was born in Chile in 1929 to a family of Jewish immigrants who had fled the pogroms of Russia. When he was 23 he emigrated to France.   It wasn’t long afterwards that he started working in Marcel Marceau’s mime troupe. Jodorowsky started hanging around Breton and his circle. Among many of his other antics, he instigated The Panic Movement, a school of transformative performance art dedicated to the ancient god Pan. In the 1950s and 60s of Paris the circles that had been built up around Gurdjieff in previous decades weren’t just a memory gone with the passing of a remarkable man, but an objective reality. Students were still around. In particular, Jeanne de Salzmann. Not only was she still alive, she lived until she was age 101, passing away in the year 1990. The work continued. (Jodorowsky himself is 97 at the time of this writing.) In the filmmakers autobiography, The Spiritual Journey of Alejandro Jodorowsky, he writes about his relationship with G.I. Gurdjieff’s purported daughter Reyna d’Assia. They had met after a screening of El Topo in Mexico City. There was instant sexual chemistry between them and they went back to her hotel. According to the story they talked about her father and his travels in India while they made love. She went on to transmit to him eighty-two different sayings that she attributed to her father. Jodorowsky wrote these down in his book. Whether or not the eighty-two saying were really part of an oral transmission from Gurdjieff to d’Assia to Jodorowsky, I’m not sure matters. They are worthy of meditation and contemplation. I tend to believe the story myself. From his fertile mind came his film Holy Mountain. Jodorowsky has always been forthright and clear on his influences, and he acknowledged how reading Daumal seeded aspects of his film into his mind. Like anything else that Jodorowsky came across, whether it was learning painting from Leonora Carrington, or taking sacred mushrooms with María Sabina, or practicing Zen Buddhist meditation with his master Ejo Takata, he was never content to simply let any one of them be end of his own spiritual quest. He kept on seeking even as he learned from these individual masters and used that knowledge to become his own master, acknowledging the genius in them, but never bowing down to any of them alone. Even so, the fingerprints of Gurdjieff and Daumal are all over his film Holy Mountain. In this movie Jodorowsky plays the roles of an alchemist to a messianic figure who has come in search of knowledge, joined by a group of figures representing the seven planetary archetypes. The alchemists puts these seekers through a series of rituals that mimic the alchemical process of transformation: calcination, where the ego gets burned asunder, preparing the way for new growth, then dissolution, the soul now untethered, into separation where different parts are further purified from one another before being brought back together again in conjunction, followed by further distillation, all culminating in the in the final stage of coagulation, the creation of the philosophers stone, inner gold. As their identities are stripped away and reforged they head to the summit of the Holy Mountain, the summit of true of knowledge, of final enlightenment. Yet in the end even this attainment is seen to be illusory. After reaching the final rung of one ladder, comes the realization that they are once again at the bottom of another. In the final part of the film, the camera turns towards the audience and the alchemist implores everyone to awaken. “Real life awaits.” It is here in this world that at our spiritual efforts must be employed. A peradam is a kind of crystalline stone described in Daumal’s novel. They are described as being  “a clear and extremely hard stone… a true crystal… harder than diamond.” A person could only discover a peradam through intense inner work. Those who sought the higher realms would be gifted with one after peak moments of realization. For the mountain guides who took people to Mount Analogue a peradam was the only payment they would take. The guitar fantasia here is a true peradam, a manifestation of intense effort and dedication to the inner work of musicianship and artistic vision. It continues on the next four shorter tracks completing this magnum opus, “The Door To The Invisible Must Be Visible,” “The Alchemist,” “21 May 1944” (this track a tribute to the day of Daumal’s death), and the “Application of Obscure Knowledge.” For those who pick up the album on Bandcamp, a third album length track is available, a remix of first “Mount Analogue” piece by PS.T. It’s a great reinterpretation of the source material and another chance to voyage upwards into liminal verticality. It finds a fitting home on the Sub Rosa label whose expansive catalog peradams in the form of discs, vinyl, and downloads suitable for the seeker who wishes to find a guide for further exploration of landscapes and vistas remain shrouded in mystery. This album is a landmark work from a master artist in tribute to the great chain of influence that goes from one seeker to another, from one artist to another. I consider it another essential clue in my own quest for discovering an applying obscure knowledge. Mount Analogue is available on Sub Rosa. items.body: Always willing to push miles ahead into abstract electronic substructures while reaching back for acid, rave, jungle, breaks, and ultra-low-end vibrations, this is music whose physical impact feels every bit as potent now as it might have in the mid-90s. Shattered, explosive and mind-numbing bass The timing for getting a new bass bin in my vehicle couldn’t have been better for Oddling Weather Forecast, an extended player and self-released gem from ΠΕΡΑ ΣΤΑ ΟΡΗ. Always willing to push miles ahead into abstract electronic substructures while reaching back for acid, rave, jungle, breaks, and ultra-low-end vibrations, this is music whose physical impact feels every bit as potent now as it might have in the mid-90s. Shattered, explosive and mind-numbing bass seems to arrive from some distant region of our galaxy. “Pocket Arctic Protocol” plunges into groundbreaking, heavily saturated breaks, with low frequencies that surround, rattle and press against everything in their path. Rather than simply sitting underneath the rhythm, bass becomes a force of its own, punching through each layer and giving every break a heavier sense of momentum. The title track doesn’t hold back on its beat artillery, throwing samples and staccato drums in all directions while those bass lines remain utterly unrelenting. They don’t merely reinforce the rhythm; they excavate foundations, shaking loose whatever is sitting on top. “Fan Failure,” meanwhile, brings a techno-breaks charge that fans of Altern 8 will consume with ease, its low-end drive keeping everything locked into a suitably frantic groove. Closing with a concentrated summary of everything that came before, “Tweezers Sizzlers (Pressure Mix)” punctuates an EP that simply doesn’t let up with throwbacks to early The Prodigy—taking our brains to another dimension. It breaks through old-school references with punching creativity, restless curiosity and bass lines powerful enough to make that new bin earn its keep. It’s made to be heard as a continuous mix, but Speake wants you to feel free to dip in and out. Speake wants you to feel free to dip in and out Photographic Memory by Speake   Speake makes handmade electronic music from London field recordings, home-built instruments, and charity-shop vinyl. Photographic Memory is essentially the city chopped fine until it stops sounding like a city and starts sounding like weather. It’s made to be heard as a continuous mix, but Speake wants you to feel free to dip in and out. The terms eidetic memory and photographic memory are often used interchangeably, a photographic memory refers to the ability to recall images, text, or objects in extreme detail with high precision after seeing them only once. Vivid mental imagery somehow impacts people’s ability for “mental time travel,” or the ability to remember past events as well as imagine future events. It is said that extensive research has failed to demonstrate consistent correlations between the presence of eidetic imagery and any cognitive, intellectual, neurological, or emotional measure. Perhaps we have developed an ability to organize certain types of information, rather than possessing an innate total recall or eidetic ability. Listen up, see what you think. “I mark but the hours of sunshine” (6:49) opens, and first something is happening in a big empty wet room, a strange munchy beat emerges, not exactly hypnotic but it does repeat in a seductive mind altering way. The liberating percussion takes away any negativity, the core stays while constantly new bits appear to add variety and sunshine, now we are building a groove. Searchlights claw the dark circle of ancient ruins :: I would like to eat sheets of rice noodles right now, stuffed with various essences, known as Cheung Fun, so smooth, slippery, soft and chewy. “No cheung fun after 5pm” (3:19) starts with a renegade commando beat, and soon the whole band moves in, bringing a blend of percussion, keyboards, odd strange sounds that repeat, a skeletal electronic clock, rumblings, and some surprise bottle play moments. “Have you ever been on a boat when you couldn’t see the land?” (5:36) Starts with ticking. Perhaps we are standing near the engine when crossing the Pacific ocean on a new kind of liner, listening to the shoveling of coal and soon a constant very steady machine is running with odd flickers of voices or phantoms. When the flow takes it down to the skeleton, soon the percussion brings it up again. Are we rowing now? Bonny hand knocks create the beat, at times someone is tossing coins or seeds or pebbles, and the machine is always running, until the arrival. This time, the motor starts right away and so we head out, “A pregnant pause” (1:40) flows along and then abruptly everything changes. “When did you stop dancing?” (8:54) enters with simulated sizzling hand tapped percussion and some electronic sparks and flares. I remember the sound made when the stylus gets to the end of the record, the vinyl windoff sound goes on and on with a hint of high hat that keeps the forward motion spicy and strong. This is followed by a title that sounds uncomfortable, “Pushing on the bit that hurts” (4:54). When the track starts, things are dark, until the sizzle walks up and away we go. The wind blows over desolate ruins and searchlights claw the dark circle of ancient ruins. I imagine riding a bike carefully down a very steep and long rocky mountain ridge at night. Sometimes the dripping sounds electronic. The crickets are playing with dry bones, tapping out musical messages, “Passing moustaches through the fence” (4:30), the piano makes this very different from what has come so far. There are Martians imitating dripping water in the cave, soon the percussion gallops along, clanking and reeling. I think there is something in the distance, we are within the machine and in the background is some more music, maybe a circus or a radio saloon. Here the piano never gets to the front and center, the clicks own us, and the crickets with those tapping bones. The final track, “Photographic Memory” (31:45), in fact is also the title track, and it turns out to be the whole album reprised as one long piece. The segues are invisible. items.body: The Sound Propositions podcast is back for a five-part mini-season exploring Big Ears 2026. Rather than another day-by-day recap (you can find that in the newsletter), or a thematic synthesis (see my 2026 review), the following five conversations sketch out a different take on the festival. Over this mini-season, we trace an arc through sacred spaces and dive bars, uncover the quiet labour of film scoring and the collective euphoria of a six-set residency. We explore what happens when a small Appalachian city becomes a vessel for music that exists nowhere else: the alchemy of exhaustion and joy, of secular drones and transcendent prayer, and the radical act of choosing your own path through 250 performances. Featuring conversations with Chuck Johnson, Gwenifer Raymond, Mary Lattimore, Booker Stardrum, and Hania Rani. Speaking of Hania Rani, her Non Fiction is among the first announcements for Unsound NYC 2026, running in late October. And Big Ears itself will be back 1-4 April 2027—keep your ears open for additional announcements. As I mentioned back when Episode 40 dropped (nearly two years ago), Sound Propositions has been on indefinite hiatus while I work on a book (and try to find a steady job). Earlier this year, I dropped the long-missing Episode 30 from back in 2023, as a hint about another mini-series that will hopefully appear this fall. You can read more about the newsletter here, and subscribe for free, where you’ll be first to hear about upcoming episodes and other projects. Until then, enjoy this look back at Big Ears 2026. Happy Listening! While their previous electronic album The Silver Cord wasn't met with overall praise, I myself was a big fan of it. But with this album it feels rather robotic and cold, and more like an experiment from only some of the band members. With more direction and a bigger conceptual grasp, it could have been more effective but it does feel like a step down from their recent output, but overall it's still fine for what it is. I'd give this a mid 6 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Sapience.

items.body: Review by proto-baldrick — The question seems to be, what differentiates this outstanding release from a Thinking Plague album? Many of the same elements are present'first of all the compositional style. Johnson's extremely distinctive and sophisticated approach to harmony and counterpoint is in evidence, where layers grate and glide against each other, disorienting the listener until background elements come to the surface and reveal the controlled and balanced design. There is also his typical fearlessness in breaking the flow with a sudden change in density and orchestration, which nonetheless maintains the tension and drive. One obvious point of distinction is the increased presence of 'classical' instruments (strings and winds), but (contrary perhaps to his intent) the overall impression is still of an expanded rock band sound rather than a rock composer's attempt at orchestral music. I find this to be a merit rather than a shortcoming.I suspect it has something to do with the people involved (though I'm never quite sure who is 'in' Thinking Plague). This relates to the orchestration and method of production, which necessarily relies heavily on remote recording as opposed to live-in-the-studio. There is also a deliberate attempt to more freely explore Johnson's classical influences. These are hard to pin down, though he has cited William Schuman as a reference. To my ear there are fleeting references here to Henri Dutilleux, and maybe even to some film composers such as Jerry Goldsmith. At times the genre approaches classical art song.The musicians are absolutely topnotch and fully up to the task of interpreting this weighty music. The rhythm section in particular is both solid and beautiful. The brass and strings shine and soar, while sitting organically in the overall texture. I have a slight issue with the vocals, which I have also noted with later Thinking Plague releases. Although much credit is due to Elaine DiFalco for her longstanding commitment to Johnson's music (how many singers would take this on?), I constantly have the impression that she is auto-tuned. It's possible that this is just a quality of her voice, but I can't help doubting it. In any case, this quality detracts ever so slightly from the organic quality of the music. It also has a bit of an obscuring effect on the lyrics, which nonetheless seem to convey a politically progressive, environmentally conscious stance (as with many Thinking Plague songs).Overall, this is a great work by (in my view) a very significant and high-level composer, not just within progressive rock but generally. My rating reflects this rather than any speculations about or imperfections in the components.

A beautiful, enveloping harmony, the deep vocals on "Light Damage"; the keyboard texture, the snarling riff before the ambient break, a gentle restart on Eric's pads leading to a violent finale. "Please be Gentle" is a cascade of luminescent keyboards gliding over the staccato vocals; rhythm, a modern, catchy prog synth-metal sound. The best part is Niccol�'s vintage keyboards on the djent riff, a far cry from the viscous RPI. The mysterious musical aura, electro on Alessandro's thick strings and the keyboards with a John Carpenter-esque feel. "The Case of the Silent Queen" is an introductory ballad, gentle and warm for the slow, melancholic build-up reminiscent of King Crimson; Drifting like a summer breeze with the grandiose piano. The synth, the heart of the sound, metronomic, on K-2000, guides this frenetic finale. A beautiful, melodic, stroboscopic moment, a voice-over, and departure into the unknown of space, a devilish, solemn metal riff."We Need to Talk," an ethereal, nursery rhyme ballad, cinematic in style, "The Love Boat"; lyrics about a couple's conversation delivered in a catchy way, a sugary pop sound as if everything were alright. "Caged" returns to a heavy, metallic sound, djent oozing over the nostalgic keyboard and piano, softening the imperial tone. Choirs amplify the sense of melancholy; an intense solo from Alessandro precedes the minimalist break. An imposing finale of sweeping choirs on this striking confinement, poised between truth and freedom. "The Day We Never Met," melancholic organ, new wave vocals, hints of XTC, Ultravox. The monolithic keyboard on the title track, a real or imagined encounter reminiscent of 10cc's sound; nostalgic. A majestic, chilling, heavy, captivating finale. "Panic Loves Telling Lies" has a groovy pop feel, Loris's bass guiding the electric crescendo in waves. Powerful and effective, rhythmic and tender.A modern prog-metal sound with sharp riffs, vintage lyrical flourishes on the Crimson King, a dark atmosphere... Cellar noise.

items.body: Review by Alxrm — The commercialization of Kansas' sound probably peaks on this album. The band was fighting to survive in the 80s environment, an environment that demanded a hit single written around the commercial approach the decade dictated which was too far from their core sound and a label on their back for the record sales (a situation described very accurately by Livgren on Mainstream). Therefore, it is a bit difficult to go down as a genuine Kansas album. Having said that, although I obviously prefer their glorious 70s body of work and also their output from Freaks of Nature and afterwards, I can't say that I dislike the album. To be exact, only Get Rich and Don't Take Your Love Away irritate me. All others range from simply good (Everybody's My Friend, Going Through the Motions) to very enjoyable (Fight Fire With Fire, Andi, End of an Age, Incident on a Bridge). Granted, you have to separate in your mind the two "different" bands or else a die-hard Kansas (and generally a prog) fan is unlikely to let the vinyl spin past the second song (and I'm generous). But, according to my taste, even when at almost full AOR mode, Kansas possess the musicality to do it with style.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There is an Argentine writer named Jos� Ingenieros who, in his book "El hombre mediocre" discussed how human development unfolds: the early years are shaped by the family environment, followed by the school environment, and later a third stage, which not everyone reaches, of self-directed learning. In this final stage, free from external influences (including the prevailing paradigm), the individual arrives at their own stance and ideas. So far, this aligns with psychoanalytic theory, but Ingenieros goes further, asserting that over time, these formative layers unravel in the reverse order of their acquisition, starting with the last one and proceeding backward until returning to childhood. Of course, the book covered other topics as well, but I read it years ago and this concept stuck with me; I recall it whenever I listen to the music and lyrics of Van Der Graaf Generator's Pawn Hearts. It is a seminal album for many reasons, both in the history of progressive rock and in Peter Hammill's career, serving as a pivotal turning point, the first of several, as is often the case with great artists.Funnily enough, it was the first album I Heard, which perhaps wasn't the ideal starting point, yet now I'm grateful for it. Even though it took some effort to digest so many complex ideas and novel approaches, it ultimately won me over completely; I felt as though I had discovered the band myself (a feeling I'm sure many others shared), and every chord became as familiar as the sounds one hears in the kitchen or the garage while growing up.If H To He, Who Am The Only One had represented a substantial step forward compared to The Least We Can Do Is Wave To Each Other, then Pawn Hearts, starting right from "Lemmings", left no doubt that we were in another galaxy: more psychedelia and, above all, a different vocal approach from Hammill, more inflections and variations serving the composition. And the composition... everything worked in perfect unison: David Jackson's sax in lockstep with Hammill, aggressive moments giving way to almost reverent pauses, and Hugh Banton's apocalyptic organ. Hammill sang operatically, wildly, lucidly, and passionately, only to switch, in the very next instant, to an agonizing, pleading wail.Just as Jackson began playing free-jazz solos, with Guy Evans providing accompaniment, Hammill would assert his high-pitched voice, surprising the listener with atonal twists. And, of course, as the keyboards entered on the same tonic, they would begin to define the classic Van Der Graaf sound; the saxophone, organ, and Hammill's vocals became the group's hallmarks, all underpinned by Guy Evans's infallible rhythm. When Peter sat at the piano, there was no stopping him (and there still isn't); it was all about attitude and sheer force of will, qualities that remain intact over the years when things are done right. "Man-Erg" is a prime example of this performance: the way the music supports the lyrics and the saxophone, the tone of the long, sustained phrasing, and then the arrival of Robert Fripp alongside Banton's keyboards, together adding color to that inferno Hammill paints with his voice strained to the absolute limit. That deep, rumbling organ... that piercing saxophone... and the drums locking into a steady rhythm... before gradually slowing down to float through a cosmic ocean, a space where everything spins until it comes full circle and meets itself. It all ties back to the album's concept and that reflection on human nature we mentioned at the start.I love those moments when the quartet would launch into an intro that felt like improvisation, stepping away from the written score to channel jazz one moment, then shifting to a classical style the next...The first thing that always grabs my attention about "A Plague of Lighthouse Keepers" is the dual vocal style Peter employs... it is as if there are two singers in one; the atmosphere grows uncanny as the music shifts from jazz and psychedelia, a grotesque chorus gaining ground and bursting into the room to paint everything with its hands, altering the very light of the space.The main suite is composed of several sections where, at times, everything turns atonal, the keyboard, the saxophone, Peter's voice, only to then shift into the sweetest melody imaginable, culminating in a masterfully written passage akin to a symphonic climax; here, his voice is pushed to previously unknown limits, for he knew no limits at the time, plunging into the most abyssal depths before soaring to where the stars are born. The final section, following the Mellotron frenzy, arrives with that piano melody and a voice that is pure, clean, powerful, and boundless; a voice that always stirs the emotions, then just as it does now (it is good that some things never change). Fripp adds atonal notes alongside the piano, while the chorus affirms that, yes, another dimension is posible, and it lies within us; it has been there all along.The meaning of Pawn Hearts may well shift over the years, but what remains constant is its musical and emotional significance, like a circle that, after spinning endlessly, returns to the same point without ever being quite the same.

items.body: Beyond Border started out as a duo in 2019 and has since grown into a trio comprising Kai Vincenz Németh, Michael Deiters, and newcomer Renee Brandt. With Aftermath, the German band delivers its third full-length album, produced by none other than Rob Dust. The album is also available as a double CD. Beyond Border remains true to a sound that sits somewhere between classic Electro-Pop and the slightly harder, more dance-oriented Future-Pop genre. Danceability is a key element of this record, an aspect undoubtedly influenced by Rob Dust’s involvement. The album is pure ‘power-pop’, occasionally incorporating guitar riffs to inject even more energy into the mix. What follows is a succession of sensational tracks, sounding like an imaginary fusion of bands such as Mesh, Massive Ego, and Depeche Mode. Terrolokaust and, notably, Ruined Conflict were invited to contribute, with the latter’s collaboration proving particularly infectious thanks to Xavier Morales and his distinctive voice. In terms of production, the album delivers everything one could expect from an Electro/Future-Pop release, while being meticulously crafted down to the finest detail. None of the twelve tracks disappoints. Small details sometimes build towards incredible climaxes, such as the female choral effect that emerges towards the end of the beautiful “Absolution”. The second disc features a solid selection of remixes, including contributions from Mesh themselves, as well as Eisfabrik and Ruined Conflict. While the Mesh and Eisfabrik remixes are my personal favorites, the more EBM-oriented remix by SK3RED also deserves a special mention. “Aftermath” is a fantastic album in every asspect, from its compositions and production to its impressive collection of remixes. As far as I’m concerned, this is an album that is bound to appear on many year-end lists of the best releases of the year. An absolute must-have!!! (Rating:9). Listen to “Absolution”:

1975年、神奈川県横須賀市生まれ。早稲田大学第一文学部卒業後、2000年よりベルリン在住。著書に『明子のピアノ』（岩波ブックレット）、監修を務めた『おとうさんのポス... 詳しく見る 音楽の友 編集部 月刊誌 1941年12月創刊。音楽之友社の看板雑誌「音楽の友」を毎月刊行しています。“音楽の深層を知り、音楽家の本音を聞く”がモットー。今月号のコンテンツはこちらバックナンバ... 詳しく見る マルヴィッツの秀でたコミュニケーション能力がコンツェルトハウス管を成功へ導く 7月8日、ヨアナ・マルヴィッツがコンツェルトハウス管弦楽団首席指揮者の任期を2032/33年シーズンまで5年間延長した。その蜜月ぶりは現地でも話題になっている。 マルヴィッツがこのポストに就任したのは2023年9月。以来、過去3シーズンの間に次々と新風を吹き込んだ。コンツェルトハウスは昨シーズンの平均稼働率を約90%と公表しているが、マルヴィッツが指揮するコンサートはほぼ毎回がソールドアウトの盛況が続いている。 その成功の大きな要因は、音楽の魅力を伝達する彼女の並外れたコミュニケーション能力にあるといえる。就任以来、コンサートの前に作品解説を行うスタイルを定着させ、ベルリンのコンサートライフの定番にまでなった。みずからピアノを弾いて聴衆に語りかけ、ときにはオーケストラを前に特定の箇所を演奏させて、聴きどころを解説する。そのエネルギッシュかつ親しみやすい語り口は自然と引き込まれるものがあり、単にわかりやすさを目指すのではなく、聴く耳を育みながら共に音楽を楽しもうという意欲にあふれる。 コンツェルトハウスのインテンダント、トビアス・レンペが、マルヴィッツについて「卓越した芸術的才能と、クラシック音楽を自然な形で魅力的に伝える能力をこれほど兼ね備えた指揮者は他にいません」と絶賛する所以だろう。 残り2シーズンを残したタイミングで、新たに5年間の契約を結ぶのも異例だ。契約更新にベルリンのカイ・ヴェーグナー市長が同席したことからも、他の都市に引き抜かれる前に確保したいという意図が透けて見える。マルヴィッツ自身は、「社会が困難な時代だからこそ、人々が共に耳を傾ける場所が必要です。今後もコンツェルトハウスが私の芸術的な拠り所であり続けることを、この上なく嬉しく思います」とコメントした。 コンツェルトハウス管の響きも、柔軟なフレージングと響きの透明さにより、室内楽的な対話を重んじるスタイルに変わりつつある。来シーズンはExpeditionskonzert（探検コンサート）のシリーズで、ベートーヴェンの交響曲を「第1番」から「第5番《運命》」まで、毎回1曲ずつというぜいたくな枠組みで取り上げる。 作品の完成度を極限まで突き詰めるペトレンコ＆ベルリン・フィルに対し、マルヴィッツ＆コンツェルトハウス管は聴衆とのコミュニケーションを重視する独自のスタイルで新たな方向性を確立した。新シーズンに始動する山田和樹＆ベルリン・ドイツ交響楽団がここにどう割って入るか。ベルリンのオーケストラ・シーンから目が離せない。 コンツェルトハウス管の「探検コンサート」で聴衆に直接語りかける指揮者のヨアナ・マルヴィッツ ©Simon Pauly ベルリンの文化生活に影を落とすシンプルな要因 ドイツの文化参加研究所（IKTf）が、昨年夏に行ったベルリンの文化イヴェントへの参加に関する調査の結果を発表した。対象となったのは、クラシックのコンサート、演劇やオペラ、バレエ、展覧会など。それによると、2023年と比較して来場者数が回復傾向にある一方、コロナ禍による長期的影響が、文化運営に依然として大きな重荷になっていることも明らかになった。 文化イヴェントへの参加においては男女間の格差も広がり、とくに50歳以上の一人暮らしの男性は、例年の調査に比べて参加の機会がますます少なくなっているという。大きな障壁の一つは、シンプルに「お金」。物価上昇のなか、回答者のほぼ3分の2（65パーセント）が「文化イヴェントへの費用を賄うのが以前より難しくなった」と答えている。入場料が障害になっていると答えた割合は、2019年の35パーセントから47パーセントへと上昇した。 IKTfがまとめた提言には、「第一に、これまでアプローチできていなかった層に対する魅力的なプログラムや解説などで伝達する要素。第二に訪れる上で壁になっている要因を取り払うこと」と書かれている。もっとも、その壁の要因になっているチケット価格を下げることは、文化予算を削減しているベルリン市の財政状況を考えると期待できない。こうした現状を鑑みると、ベルリン市にとっても「希望の星」であるマルヴィッツの異例ともいえる早期の契約更新の背景が浮かんでくる。

items.body: Nagoya’s leftfield electronic scene has recently garnered interest from the international music press. This is chiefly thanks to the efforts of producer and all-around scenester Yuya Abe (abentis). abentis has been an associate of Facta & K-LONE’s Wisdom Teeth label since 2021. After a chance encounter with Facta on the platform formerly known as Twitter, Wisdom Teeth featured abentis’ track “Bicycle” in their 2022 compilation To Illustrate. Earlier this year, abentis curated a compilation of Nagoya talent for Wisdom Teeth titled nagoyaka na kaze / 和やかな風 (quiet wind). Entries oscillate from woodblock percussion-fronted minimal house to rootsical UK bass. Now the artist returns with his debut album Dim Grow, the first physical release on his fledgling 2++ label, which he plans to use to promote the Nagoya scene. Dim Grow is fairly short, clocking in at just 41 minutes, but contains enough unique ideas to fill a longer work. “Separate” opens the album with an unhurried cavalcade of brassy splashes and arpeggiation evoking Italian experimentalist Caterina Barbieri. It segues into “In Memories,” the longest piece on Dim Grow at just over nine minutes. It’s maybe too long; physically modeled kalimba dominates the first 90 seconds until the rising tedium is suddenly leavened with bass. A Steve Reich influence looms large for the remaining seven-plus minutes, a twinkling tropical variation on the American minimalist composer’s studied drift between melodic and rhythmic phrases. Especially compelling are the reverberant marimba stabs near the end with a series of showy decay accents—essentially the audio equivalent of crisp serifs. “Far Enough” and “Lune,” channel some of abentis’ Japanese influences, particularly goopy analog synth leads reminiscent of Thousand Knives-era Ryuichi Sakamoto and Haruomi Hosono’s late 70s prog-psych experiments—albums like Cochin Moon and Paraiso that détourned western exotica-kitsch. “Far Enough” is particularly mischievous; one motif is teasing a trap-style snare line only to collapse it into a wash of static. Forays into dance music shade the second half of Dim Grow. The swung 4/4 of “Lune” could earn it a place in a more open-minded house or techno set. “Eachpath” susurrates with the restlessness of 2010s deconstructed club artists like Jam City and Lee Gamble, but grounded in the rhythmic and harmonic grooves of 90s intelligent techno acts like B12, Ken Ishii, and LA Synthesis. “Circulation” is the shortest track on the album and may also be the most dance-oriented: bedroom techno with dubby mallet percussion running in opposite directions over male voices that lie on the threshold of discernibility. It’s easy to envision this music issuing from the soundsystem of a chic Nagoya(ka) sake bar, and if abentis gets his way, audiophile venues the world over. (Marcello Ursic)

items.body: Review by Steve Conrad — An Apocalyptic COVID-Confectionary ConstructionApocalyptic: "Relating to or predicting widespread destruction or the collapse of civilization." (American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language).I mean, look at this cover art- it positions the Rock Boutique as the last outpost of...something...before one ventures into the apocalyptic wilderness- the Elon Musk-esque rocket ship preparing to exit the planet (whichever planet this may be), the more-angular St. Louis arch, the slightly blood-shot mechanical eye in full surveillance mode, and the almost confectionary-appearing glowing purple...objects, which are (menacingly?) beginning to multiply within Morri's domain.And the "wheel in the sky"- biblical Ezekiel reference- and yes, what the heck is that reference? While the stream (with fiery twinkles) wends its way through the landscape.The COVID-ConfectionSo, on this third album from Chicago, USA's "progressive rock collective, REFESTRAMUS, the stage is set for the seven (on Bandcamp, nine) tracks featured on "Morri's Rock Boutique).I'm hearing these tracks- whichever version of the album you choose- as "COVID-Confection" since according to the band's bio- drummer/songwriter/lyricist Derek Ferguson formed the first incarnation of REFESTRAMUS during the initial onslaught of the worldwide global scourge of COVID, and the music on this album at least for me- an early progressive rock geek- reeks of the sort of touches that made Styx a lot of money, as well as the grandeur and flourishes that endeared many of us folks-of-a-certain-age to the progressive genre.I remember a faintly condescending review (probably in Rolling Stone, which in those days was holy writ for me) of one of the 70's era KANSAS albums, in which the all-knowing reviewer said something like, "it's fairly decent music, but with wedding-cake arrangements". Little did this reviewer know that these "wedding cake" arrangements were exactly what made some of us geeks sit up and pay attention!Which is to say that on this album, where are many "confectionary" sections that delight an aging geek, and might delight you as well, regardless of your age and geekiness. Keyboardist/vocalist Dyanne Potter Vogetlin provides standout synth and keyboard fills and flourishes that genuinely soar, that color the overall sound with richness and verve. One can hear this almost from the very beginning of the album.To this reviewer, the bass guitar and vocal prowess of Jan Christiana are almost other-worldly. Upon first hearing, I wondered who on earth could actually sing that high, with that kind of power and control? Well, Jan can. I suspect Jan also has a lot to do with the vocal arrangements, which are lush and varied, and become an additional "unsung" instrument in the confectionary construction of "Morri's Rock Boutique".So yes, even on the opening "Storms" and then certainly on the (Russian folk tale-based) "The Cossack's Dream", we get the kind of grandeur and sweep of early era progressive and glam-rock music. I had to think of AVIARY and of course Styx, sometimes even Queen due to the vocal flourishes.None of this is to diminish or minimize the contributions of each musician- it is a "rock collective" of accomplished musicians who play supremely well together, and given a spacious production by Ian Beaubout. The variety of approaches on this album is also worth mentioning, including the Russian, and later the Asian touches complete with instrumentation like shamisen, koto, and shakuhachi found on "Lakeview Samurai"- engagingly sung by Nam Chumo.Lakeview Samurai appeals to me like confection- surface sweetness, not so much substance. I can get the references to some of the current cultural scene, and the side-by-side transposition of the ancient and venerable samurai code. Everything is done well, it simply doesn't touch me very deeply, nor perhaps, fit within the framework of this album.Same goes for "Hell or NYC", pointing out the stereotypes (and perhaps well-deserved) of the coldness and rudeness of the vast population of that enormous and varied city. The sax touches and the film-noir story-telling is captivating- yet still, confection, for better or worse.I guess the themes being explored allow different interpretations- for me, the overall affect of the collection of tracks is that it seems like "pastiche", rather than coherent whole- in the sense of the "hodgepodge" definition of pastiche. And maybe that's Derek's point and his intention.In ConclusionIt's excellently done, catchy, filled with verve and variety, demonstrating fine musicianship from each participant in this production- progressive rock luminaries and newcomers too. AND at the same time, for better or worse, confectionary. I'm going with 3.5 candied stars, but rounding up to 4 thanks to the overall fine effort given.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Cornwall's anachronistic Arthurian spacemen return with their seventh full-length studio album release since their formation (in Edinburgh) in 2010 and second in two years (which is unusually fast for them). 1. "Song of the Rainforest" (21:20) a vocal-less and more keyboard-generated epic than the usual Emerald Dawn offerings. Also, it feels as if the presence and contributions of Dave Greenaway and Tom Jackson here are on the same level of importance (and dynamics) as those of Ally and Tree. (36/40)- i. "Balance" - after a long 90-second intro of cave dripping sounds and two alternating sustained organ chords slowly establishing their pace and fullness and then the entrance and establishment of bass and drums into an awesome funk-lite vamp groove of two gorgeous Mellotron-like chords Ally enters with his seering electric guitar to deliver one of his best guitar solos ever--for five minutes! The contagious groove established by Dave Greenaway and Tom Jackson is awesome. - ii. Incursions - a stop-and-pause precedes a very slow switch to Smooth Reggae groove over which Ally solos with his tenor sax. As Trees synth strings enter (and Ally's tenor sax desists), the beat is sped up (we're now into the ninth minute), which prompts Ally to switch to his soprano sax--which gives Tree a little more room and license to embellish with her variety of synth strings riffs: often matching or meeting Ally's sax lines with her own.- iii. "Loss" - in the 11th minute another interlude of synth strings intervals paves the way for a heavier, almost ominous motif to set up with Tom's more tribalistic tom-tom-centered (synthetic talking drum?) drumming and Dave's heavily-wowed bass play being stomped over by some deep monster-saw keyboard and guitar riffs. The keyboards continue riffing--kind of soloing--for a couple of minutes over this motif before . . . - iv. "Regret" - the 14th minute has the establishment of a peaceful, perhaps sad motif of jungle/tropical sounds (including Tree's Amazonian flute) woven loosely around one another until the 18th minute when saw synth chords take over and Ally returns to shredding emotionally on his guitar. One of the most evocative, sensitive, and surprisingly tight--even thoughtful--sections of any Emerald Dawn song I've ever encountered. 2. "Rivers of Tears" (14:58) opens with a jaunty journey of jazz-classical-sounding solo piano play. Among the most impressive and pretty keyboard play I've ever heard from Tree! At 1:40 bass, drums, and, eventually, Ally's "reverberated-into-the-background" electric guitar slowly enter. Tree continues to tinkle the ivories within and behind the guitar, bass, and drums while adding some washes of synth strings to the mix as Ally continues shredding (as he does). Then Ally stops, making room for Tree to expand her piano note play as Tom and Dave slowly, gradually slow down and drop out. a pause/break at 3:30 results in the unleashing of Tree's reverb-drenched voice over only the banks of synth strings chords and still tinkling piano note play (mostly in progressing arpeggios)--which eventually becomes just synth strings as we enter into another little pause around 5:30. Here Tree establishes a chord progression with the repetition of four descending arpeggiated chords over which the rhythm section joins in and Ally deploys his tenor sax. Another pause at the seven-minute mark leads into a transference of the play of the descending chord pattern to synth strings as Tom and Dave kick back and Ally switches to electric guitar. Here Dave's bass playing is a bit rote and uninventive while the embellishments that Tom adds to his drumming feel a bit forced and "required" while Ally's guitar shredding sounds/feels . . . the same as ever. A little pause at the end of the tenth minute is filled with Tree's vocal lines until the band re-emerges with a kind of two-chord "tropical" vamp. Yet another stop and transition at 11:45 as the band shifts into a much more dark and ominous section--launched off as Tree shouts out a "Poison. Into. It's veins." declaration. This section could almost be coming from NIL or KING CRIMSON--even with Tree's operatic high-note repeat delivery of the word "poison." The motif then morphs in the second half of the 14th minute into something more akin to a Led Zeppelin descending chord progression--which it plays out to the song's end with embellishing accents coming from Ally's synths and Tom's drums. Not bad! (26.375/30)- i. "The Natural Cycle" - ii. "Disruption" 3. "Paradise" (8:56) opening with some excitingly pregnant synthesizer play--chords, bass, and peppy upper register riffs--which subside when Tree's plaintive, melancholy voice enters at 0:33 to introduce the song's theme. By the one minute mark she pauses wherein Tom and Mark enter with a cool, jazzy, STING "Englishman in New York"-like motif (which then happens to support Tree's "Englishman in New York" vocal melody lines). Nice bass line beneath Tree's organ chords as Ally enters with a bluesier Gilmour-like approach to his injections of guitar riffs and flurries. Around the four-minute mark the band slows things down, Tree's voice softens, while Mark and Tom's play kind of moves into greater prominence as Ally and Tree's keyboard play slides more into the background of the mix. Interesting! And I like it: I like having the bass and drums mixed in front of the keys, guitars, and saxes. The synth strings and guitar soloing in the next two minutes feel much more like the sound palette of Polish NeoProg masters COLLAGE's great textures on their Moonshine masterpiece (especially "The Blues"). In the seventh minute one of the keys begins to repeat and develop a melody line from THE MOODY BLUES' "Nights in White Satin," to which Tom backs down for a bit, but then everybody ramps up again into a fully-COLLAGE motif in which the synth strings continue soloing as other synth chords continue to deploy the "Nights in White Satin" chords and melody-reminders. Brilliant! And this is how they choose to end the song, the album! Awesome! Despite the "borrowing" of the sound palette and melody/chords, I finally feel as if The Emerald Dawn have arrived to the gates of top-tier prog, the symphonic side! (18.75/20)- i. "Losing Paradise"- ii. "Harmony Regained"Total Time 45:14I like the more sophisticated complexities ED are injecting into their compositions as it diminishes the dreaded monotony wrought of their old style of endlessly jamming over simple and often drawn-out single- and/or double-chorded vamps. Either their music theory has improved or they've decided to let go of the stoner-rock approach to song-rendering and employ more symphonic structuring for their music--whatever it is, I like it!A-/4.5 stars; a stunningly-improved advancement of compositional design yields the best album of The Emerald Dawn's career--one that has them knocking on the door of the Valhalla of the Symphonic Prog masters! I'm bumping up this rating into masterpiece status for the surprising display of growth as well as this being, in my opinion, Emerald Dawn's best album yet.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 982Le Orme is one of the longest lasting and best known Italian progressive rock bands. Le Orme was formed in Venice in 1966 by Aldo Tagliapietra (voice and guitars), Nino Smeraldi (guitars), Claudio Galietti (guitar and bass) and Marino Rebeschini (drums). Their first album, "Ad Gloriam" was released in 1968. From their psychedelic and beat initial roots, the band moved into much more increasingly sophisticated musical structures. In that line, the band released two excellent albums "Collage" in 1971 and "Uomo Di Pezza" in the following year. Their 1973 album "Felona E Sorona" is widely regarded as one of the top albums in the Italian progressive rock scene. By this time, the band consisted of Tagliapietra (mostly on bass with some guitar) along with keyboard player Tony Pagliuca and drummer Michi Dei Rossi."Felona E Sorona - Deluxe Edition (English And Italian Versions)" is a very special compilation album of Le Orme that was released in 2011. This is an economic package that includes their fourth studio album "Felona E Sorona", released in 1973, in its original Italian version, and their fifth studio album, which is the same album but in its English version and that was also released in the same year. This can be a very interesting compilation album because it includes the two versions of the album. As many of us know, "Felona E Sorona" is in general considered the best work from the band and is also considered a landmark to Italian progressive rock as one of the best and most important progressive rock albums ever made, especially in the Italian progressive rock scene. So, what we have really here is a great album in its two versions, probably at a cheaper price, and what will be a very worthwhile purchase, especially for those who are collectors and huge fans of Le Orme, fans of the Italian progressive rock or fans of the great prog music in general.As I'm going to review these two albums on Progarchives, in a more extensive way, I'm not going to do it at this moment. So, if you are interested to know, in more detail, what I'll write about them later, I invite you to read both of my reviews, in time. However, here I'm going to write something about them in a shorter way. So, of course, I'm not going to analyze them track by track, as I'm going to do, but I'm only going to make a global appreciation of both albums."Felona E Sorona" - Italian Version: "Felona E Sorona" is one of the classic albums of the Italian prog rock scene. The album quickly reached the top of the Italian charts giving the band their second gold record. Like many others, I find "Felona E Sorona" to be Le Orme's most fascinating work. In less than 35 minutes, Le Orme delivers probably their greatest masterpiece. Their high level of musicianship is evident over the all album. The focus is more on mood, song structure, and texture. As a concept work and despite the nine pieces, mostly short pieces and with a lot of variety, the album sounds very homogeneous and less like a collection of individual songs. This is an album that still has a strong influence in the world of progressive rock to the point that La Maschera Di Cera paid tribute to it by extending its theme and even going so far as to take up and transform the superb original cover. "Felona E Sorona" is a true classic of the movement and it's unforgivable not to have it if you like Italian prog rock. "Felona E Sorona" is an absolute must-buy."Felona E Sorona" - English Version: "Felona E Sorona" is a beautiful album, soaked with that 70's flavour that we all prog rock fans love. Although it's by no means technical, the band presents a unique sound that combines vocal parts that exude a unique sense of song with dramatic instrumental parts that make full use of synths and organs to portray a variety of scenes, including lyricism and thrills. It's an album of the golden years of progressive. Like their compatriots Premiata Forneria Marconi and Banco Del Mutuo Soccorso, "Felona E Sorona" was also released in the original Italian version and in the English version. At the request of Tony Stratton-Smith the owner of Charisma Records, Le Orme recorded an English version of the album with lyrics translated by Peter Hammill. It was also entitled "Felona E Sorona" and was also released in 1973. The English album is very similar, except that the vocals were more expressive and appropriate in Italian. This English version is also very good but listen to the Italian version because it's much better.Conclusion: Italian and English versions of the album give the listener the opportunity to hear the English lyrics, and yet enjoy the authentic feel of the original album. Well written notes in both Italian and English, including song lyrics. The essay in these notes gave me a proper understanding of what this album is about, as well as details about the album's production. As a bonus, there are also some band photos and copies of original mixes and vinyl stickers, both English and Italian. However, there's a poor sound quality for the English version. The volume is lower than that of the Italian version, which is a pity. Besides, I strongly prefer the Italian vocals to the English. I think escape to us some of the most important parts of the original album, which are the vocals. I can understand why many people, especially the non-Latin language speakers, prefer the English version. But, definitely, the original is always better than the copy.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: I’m dying In your Subterranean World Geranium eye Kiss of the poison flower There are dreams in which we run from monsters, and others in which the monster is time itself. You move through a room of people arrested between gestures, mouths open around unfinished words, hands suspended above tables, faces fixed by some invisible Mombi whose spell has spared only you. At first, there is curiosity. Then comes the dreadful privilege of observation. You notice how strange a human being becomes when deprived of motion, how life resides in the smallest continuation. And as you weave among them, one thought follows closely behind: perhaps they are not frozen. Perhaps you are passing. Los Angeles artist Blone Noble has spent 2026 behaving as though settling on one particular musical identity might constitute a misdemeanor. After May’s Dominator EP pushed New Beat, industrial, and Italo into the club, the eerie Subterranean World, co-written and produced by Dakota Blue, takes the stranger route: down the trapdoor, past the plumbing, and into an underworld where romance has acquired pincers. Noble describes the collaboration, though the music suggests dangerous laboratory conditions: “Dakota Blue and I have been working in the shadows for some time now, developing a new musical language in his Pasadena studio; a neo-futuristic art rock record built on primal rhythms, eastern synths, fretless wanderings and LA noir poetry. We wrote and recorded Subterranean World in our first session together.” That Mick Karn fixation makes itself known through Blue’s fretless bass, which prowls rather than anchors, carrying echoes of Dali’s Car, Japan, Bryan Ferry’s Bête Noire, and Talk Talk’s The Colour Of Spring without turning the song into a museum tour. Noble’s droning vocal inhabits the music with the calm of somebody describing his poisoning while deciding the flowers were worth it. The lyrics take erotic obsession underground, where devotion means accepting humiliation, death, poverty, insects, occult initiation, and whatever other indignities love has stored in the basement. Romance has rarely sounded so eager to be eaten alive. Director Redamo Rosa gives that delirium an unnerving visual form. His camera passes through bizarre tableaux populated by people frozen, as though Medusa had wandered through a Twilight Zone episode and decided everyone needed to hold still for continuity. Bodies become mannequins, gestures hang unfinished, and rooms acquire the logic of a bad dream you understand until breakfast. “I had this idea to have a camera move through dreams, almost like walking through a museum or diorama of a reality, only this reality is slightly bent,” Rosa explains. “I didn’t want there to be any reason behind the visuals, but I wanted the audience to feel disoriented by what they’re seeing. Often, we find deep meaning in inexplicable dreams. I approached Blone Noble with the idea, and he played Subterranean World for me. The song captured that feeling I was chasing – it played like narration to a nightmare and felt like it was about the darkest parts of humanity.” The result feels deliciously wrong, a surreal dip in the darkest shadows of our psyches, where everybody else has stopped moving and the camera, cursed with consciousness, keeps going.
