マティアス・シュルツ新総裁が就任して10カ月、ほんとうに目が回るような興味深い公演が途切れることなく続いたチューリヒ歌劇場の初シーズンが終わった。もともと月に1回は新演出を発表する劇場であったが、そこに新フェスティヴァルが加わり、シーズンオープニングには24時間劇場を開放して、舞台上で泊まるという体験もできた。 締めくくりは3日間連続の「Opernhaus für Alle」で、1日目はバレエ公演、2日目はオペラ公演を劇場前広場の大スクリーンに映し出し、無料で観られるイヴェントに加え、今年は3日目に初めてライヴ・コンサートも催された。 6月26日は36℃の猛暑のため1時間遅らせ、今季から当劇場のプリンシパルダンサーとしてドレスデン州立歌劇場から引き抜かれた綱木彩葉がヒロインを踊る《ロメオとジュリエット》が大きく映し出された。 27日は先月レポートしたワーグナー《タンホイザー》、そして28日はジャナンドレア・ノセダ音楽監督が指揮する歌劇場管弦楽団がバンジャマン・ベルナイムを迎え、この広場完成時の2014年以来12年ぶりのオープンエアコンサートとなった。ビゼー「《カルメン》前奏曲」で始まり、ベルナイムは〈花の歌〉で、来年のドン・ホセ初役の準備を着々と進めていることをうかがわせた。次はグノーに移り、《ファウスト》のバレエ音楽のあと、《ロメオとジュリエット》からアリア〈昇れ、太陽よ〉を抒情的に歌った。最後はマスネで、《タイスの瞑想曲》をコンサートマスターのバルトゥオメイ・ニジョウのソロもふくめて甘く聴かせたあと、マスネ《ウェルテル》の〈オシアンの歌〉でドラマティックに前半を終えた。後半はドヴォルジャーク「交響曲第9番《新世界より》」で華々しく幕を閉じた。 テテルマンの主演でアルミリアートが指揮したチューリヒ歌劇場の《ウェルテル》 上述のベルナイムが当劇場の前シーズンで好演したマスネ《ウェルテル》。2018年のプレミエ時にピョートル・ベチャワが歌い、そしてフアン・ディエゴ・フローレス、ベルナイムと、どんどんフランス・オペラらしく研ぎ澄まされてきたが、今年は今話題を集めているテノール、ジョナサン・テテルマンの主演でマルコ・アルミリアートが指揮し、プッチーニのようなドラマティックなアプローチで魅せた。フレーズの歌わせかたもロマンティックで、テテルマンの取り憑かれたような激情によく合う。「フランス・オペラらしくない」と一刀両断されればそれまでだが、心を鷲掴みにされることは否めない。シャルロッテ役のアンナ・ゴリャチョーワは、そんな骨太な主人公と比べても太すぎる声で、どうしてもこの役になじめない。アルベール役のアクセル・ダヴェヤンとソフィ役のチェルシー・ツルフリューは好演した（所見日：7月1日）。 チューリヒ歌劇場の《コジ・ファン・トゥッテ》から。舞台上に作られた2階建ての建物 ©Monika Ritterhaus そして7月3日に初見したモーツァルト《コジ・ファン・トゥッテ》も、同じく2018年にキリル・セレブレンニコフが演出したプロダクションだ。映画監督でもある視点から、まず舞台上に2階建ての建物を作り、男性陣と女性陣の会話をうまく分けたり、恋人を取り替えるときに黙役に演技させ、歌手は黒子のように側で歌う方法をとった。視覚的にはひじょうに楽しめる舞台となっているが、音楽的にはドタバタしてしまうところも多かった。また、最後の種明かしの際、元の恋人に殺し文句を歌うのが不可解だった。 ヴィンタートゥール・ムジークコレギウムと、来季で首席指揮者契約が終わるロベルト・ゴンザレス=モンハスは若々しいモーツァルトを聴かせたが、オペラに慣れていないため、牽引力が足らない。 今宵のいちばんの歓びは、フェッランドを歌うボグダン・ヴォルコフを聴けたことだ。初めて聴いたときから注目していたが、重い役を歌ったせいで光らないこともあったため、これからもレパートリーに気をつけてもらいたい。ドン・アルフォンゾ役のルカ・ピサローニも重めの役だとくすぶるので、このような役で輝き続けてほしい。フィオルディリージ役のエルベニータ・カイタツィは低音も安定し、余裕の歌唱と演技を見せ、初役とは思えなかった。ドラベッラ役のシエナ・リヒト=ミラーも初役で健闘したが、2022年から当歌劇場のアンサンブル歌手として活躍しているものの、歌唱力が今一つ伸びない。反対にグリエルモ役のヤニック・デブスは2024年からアンサンブルに入ったが、このところ伸びてきている。レベカ・オルヴェーラは、なんとか頑張ってデスピーナを演じた。

items.body: It is Monday morning, checkout time at Grand Hotel Viljandi, and a German festival goer with his wristband still on hands back his room card and asks what a double costs. Not for tonight, he specifies, for the same weekend next July, when Viljandi Folk comes round again, and preferably the very same room he has just spent four nights in. The receptionist explains that the system will not take a booking more than 11 months out. He takes this badly. He has plainly been turning it over for a while, perhaps since Thursday’s wild folk dances, perhaps during the downpour on Sunday night just before the grand finale, and now there is nothing to be done with the thought except carry it home.  That is a fairly standard state to leave Viljandi in. The town has something to do with it. Seventeen thousand people live on a ridge above a long glacial lake in southern Estonia, forest running down to the water on the far shore and the ruins of a 13th-century Livonian Order castle at the centre, the ground falling away in wide grass terraces cut by deep ravines. Those terraces are the festival: four outdoor stages sitting in the folds of the hills, Kaevumägi (Well Hill) at the top, the two Cherry Hills (Kirsimägi I & II) below it, and the Song Festival Grounds down on the flat. Two indoor rooms handle the rest: the Traditional Music Centre beside the ruins, the Ait or granary as locals call it, and the Sakala Centre in town, carrying the quieter programme by day and the wilder dances by night. Everything is ten minutes’ walk from everything else. To cross between Kaevumägi and the ruins you take the suspension bridge, 50 metres of it slung over a 13-metre trench and still swaying under everyone who steps on. Black sheep graze the slopes throughout, unbothered by any of it. And the festival is not only up on the ticketed grounds. It spills straight down into the old town, where two free stages run from lunchtime to eleven at night across all four days: the Green Stage on Laidoneri Square, where the dance schools set out workshops so anyone can learn the steps, and Sõprade Hoov on Lossi Street, a village-party yard open to any musician who fancies a turn. Seventy concerts happen out here, matching the paying stages exactly, strung along a street lined with a craft and design market where nobody checks a wristband. The programmed players are only half of it. Buskers of every age sprout across town, under gazebos and on pavements, some barely tall enough to hold the instrument, playing to whoever slows down. What carries across those slopes, alleyways and squares is pärimusmuusika, a word the English ‘folk’ flattens badly. For four days in late July this town does not commemorate its traditions so much as live inside them and shove them somewhere new. Most of what you hear sits on archival foundations: village fiddle tunes, bagpipe repertoire, regilaul runic song, the older Estonian and Finno-Ugric layers that were collected, catalogued and came within a generation of vanishing. Yet none of it is handled as museum material. This year’s theme, ‘To Each Their Own Instrument,’ was taken literally. Stages were packed with uncommon, traditional instruments most people couldn’t name, and within a day half of them were queuing to try one. Inside the Ait, the festival kept a second timetable. On three of the four nights, Thursday, Friday and Saturday, its great hall turned into Tantsumaja, the dance house, running from around 11pm until three or four in the morning while a rotating cast of folk musicians kept the tunes coming in relay. What happened on the floor was not a taught routine so much as a shared fluency: circles and couples moved through the room side by side, skill levels visibly ranging from a first attempt to real virtuosity, yet the general standard stayed remarkably high, dancers who had grown up on this repertoire picking out the shape of a tune they had never heard before and finding the steps inside it before the first verse was out. It all began, as it always does, with the parade winding through town on the Thursday early afternoon, before mayor Jaak Pihlak handed the ceremonial key to festival chief Ando Kiviberg, who has run this since its first edition in 1993. Just over 7,000 people came through the gates across that afternoon and evening, more day-one pass buyers than last year. In the Ait, six students turned the theme into a play, To Each Their Own Instrument, staged by director Lee Taul with a cast drawn from the Viljandi Culture Academy, the Estonian Academy of Music and Theatre and Tartu’s Eller college. Bagpipe, kannel and Teppo-type accordion were carried through the story by players still young enough to be studying them, the archive walking and talking rather than sitting in a case. The same idea took physical form a few streets over, on Pikk Street beside St John’s Church, where Pilliküla opened to the public for the first time: an ‘instrument village’ of close to 80 free workshops where anyone could sit down with a teacher and coax a first note out of a kannel, a bagpipe, a jaw harp, a fiddle, a talharpa or an accordion. “Musical heritage lives on as long as playing an instrument is common enough among the people,” Kiviberg said of the idea behind Pilliküla, the point being that a tradition survives by being played, not preserved. You could see the results all over town that weekend. Children busked on the hills and street corners with whatever they could play, one girl of maybe twelve and her violin set up between two stages with her case open for coins, taking more by evening than some of the market stalls. Up on the stages, the theme got loud. On II Kirsimägi that first afternoon, Gangar dug century-old dance tunes out of Norway’s national archives and ran them through a rock band. The Oslo five-piece build off springar and gangar rhythms, the old triple-time and walking dances they take their name from, Hardanger fiddle ringing over a rhythm section that a rhythm section hammering underneath, and drive the lot flat out. They played here in 2022, so they knew the crowd would dance, and it did. Down on the Song Festival Grounds, the sounds pulled from much further away. The Zawose Queens held the first Tanzanian booking in Viljandi’s history, and the sky opened just as they were due on, the kind of delay that empties a field. It did not. People pulled up hoods and waited, and by the time Pendo Zawose and her niece Leah came on, the wait had sharpened the air: Wagogo polyphony over ilimba thumb pianos and chizeze fiddle, a London rhythm section laying psychedelic rock beneath, a rain-soaked crowd that had chosen to be there. Their grandfather Hukwe Zawose carried this music around the world but never once let the women of his family sing lead; two generations on, his daughter and granddaughter stood at the front of the stage. The rain never really let up on the first evening, and neither did the appetite for dancing in it. Manhu closed Kaevumägi from half nine, five Sani players from the farming villages of the Stone Forest of Yunnan, together since 2003. They build from the lusheng, a bamboo mouth-organ whose drone sets the whole thing running, then stack the three-string adiza and call-and-response singing on top, with bass and drum kit worked so far underneath that the village music always keeps the upper hand. This is the sound of Sani daily life, drinking songs, welcome songs, love songs, seasonal tunes, nearly all of it built to move to, and they run a set the same way: a tune, a stop to walk the crowd through the steps, then the tune again, faster. Not a full sentence of English passed between the five of them and none was needed. One lifted a single leaf to his lips and bent a melody out of it; the steps were called by demonstration, arms up, follow this. By the last stretch a cold, soaked Estonian crowd that had never heard Sani music in its life was strung across the grass doing Yunnan courtship dances in the rain. Outdoors, the weather could be worn like a badge. Indoors, it exposed the festival’s one real weakness. Early shows had already packed the Ait to the walls. Over at the Sakala Centre, TõnisMägi, whose “Koit” became an anthem of the 1988 Singing Revolution, sold out fast enough to leave a queue stranded at a closed door, though these days the noise around him owes as much to his divisive public stances as to his songs. It happened repeatedly over the next three days: too many people, too few seats, and indoor rooms never built for crowds this size. Friday opened, in the early afternoon, on Ruhnu, with music and tales that had come closer than most to disappearing for good. Sounds and Stories from Ruhnu Island takes its name from a speck in the Gulf of Riga, Runö in Swedish, that held a few hundred ethnic Swedes and their own fiddle tradition until 1944, when the Soviet advance emptied the island almost overnight and left the repertoire alive only on tape. Fiddlers Karoliina Kreintaal and Lee Taul, with storyteller Kairi Leivo, have spent years playing it back off those recordings, and here they did it as a one-off. Ruhnu-born storyteller Jüri Keskpaik told the island’s life from the inside, its weddings, feasts, church and sea, while three members of the Nordic supergroup Groupa sat in: fiddler Mats Edén, flautist Jonas Simonson, and Terje Isungset, the Norwegian percussionist who builds his instruments from wood, stone and ice, all three back on Kaevumägi a few hours later for Groupa‘s own set. Behind them the whole time ran the island itself, archive film of Ruhnu’s shoreline, its people, customs and dances, a vanished community moving on screen while its own tunes played live underneath. Later that afternoon Mari Kalkun, born and raised in the Võru country of Estonia’s south-east and one of the few keeping its endangered Võro language sung, brought her kannel up against the kokle of Latvian player Laima Jansone. The kannel and the kokle are cousins, box zithers grown from the same ancient Baltic instrument and drifted so far apart that their traditions barely recognise one another now. Set them back together and that separation is nowhere to be heard: Kalkun’s playing drifting and psychedelic, her voice carrying the Võro songs she has spent a career prising out of the archive, against Jansone’s harder, more rhythmic attack, the two instruments circling, answering, now and then locking into a single line as though they had never parted. Then Kalkun left the stage entirely, microphone in hand, and walked into the middle of the field to sing from there, the crowd falling quiet and closing around her as she moved. In the evening, Amaro Duho kept their tradition in the family, literally. Matild Dobi assembled the band in 2021 from her own children, four decades after she helped start Ando Drom, one of the great names in Hungarian Roma music, and the point was to hold the songs together rather than let them scatter. It showed. Oláh Roma tradition on guitar, tambura and accordion, their own tunes threaded through the inherited ones, all of it played with the loose, unforced ease of people who do this around a table at home and happened, that night, to be doing it in front of a few thousand strangers. Estonian tradition can be handled far less gently, and Mandoterror proved it: a distorted rhythm section and a mandolin screaming where a lead guitar should be, five players who take Estonian folk melody and hit it at Nordic-metal weight. Kristjan Kuusmik stood out front on vocals, Tanel Sakrits‘ mandolin carrying the tunes a fiddle would usually hold, the old material cranked through songs from last year’s Nõiajaht and the anthem ‘Oru Leeni’. There is no compromise in it. The melodies land as though they were originally written for the extra volume: fast, sharp, and carrying clean across the grounds. The bigger stages found their real heat once it got dark, starting with Zetod on the Song Festival Grounds, the set that, by the reckoning of more or less everyone there, was where the festival properly began. Formed in Värska in 2003, they take Seto leelo, the old polyphonic singing of Estonia’s south-eastern border country, and play it at the speed and volume of a punk band: short hard songs stacked back to back, every word in Seto dialect, the pit moving from the first number and a whole field firing the lines back. In keeping with the year’s theme they built the set around four fiddles, one apiece, over accordion, bass and drums, the old dance tunes and archive material driven hard and fast. The singing that once went slow and unaccompanied, one voice leading and the rest answering, comes out here distorted and double-time, and nobody down the front drops a syllable. Most of the pull is frontman Jalmar Vabarna, who has fronted the band since they were teenagers and, off the stage, happens to be the elected ülemsootska, earthly stand-in for the Seto king. Same job either way, really, carrying his own corner of the country in front of as many people as will have it. By Saturday the site was full, 11,000 through the gates and the biggest crowd of the four days, the paths between stages packed from early afternoon as people wove from one set to the next. It all spilled onto the Song Festival Grounds, where HrayBery had the whole arena linking hands. The Polish-Ukrainian band rebuild village dance music from old scores and field recordings of the San river valley, a border region of eastern Galicia once shared by Poles, Ukrainians, Jews and Roma before post-war deportations scattered its people. They looked the part, in the Sunday best of a century ago: straw boater hats over dark suits and waistcoats for the men, high-collared white blouses and pale skirts for the women. Two fiddles, hammered dulcimer and frame drum drove the kolomyjkas, mazurkas, polkas and kozaks, and the crowd read the cue: great circling chains across the concrete, ring inside ring, while the grass banks behind filled with people watching them turn. A couple of hours later, still on the Grounds, the picture shrank from a full folk band to two women over a single instrument. Duo Ruut are Ann-Lisett Rebane and Katariina Kivi, who sit facing each other across one kannel, close enough to touch, one plucking while the other bows or drums the body, their voices soaring into harmonies that can hold a field still. Here they broke that on purpose, billing the set as Duo Ruut³ and pulling in Indrek Mällo on bass, Jaan Jaago on electric guitar, and on percussion Tõnu Tubli, who drummed a decade in Trad.Attack! and had already remixed the duo’s tunes on his own record. Outdoors, the expanded setup carried and got people moving, but it cost something too: the fine, quiet tension of two players negotiating one instrument is what makes them extraordinary, and a rhythm section inevitably paints over it. Still, once a real beat was locked under the runo song, the Grounds went from hushed to dancing. Over on II Kirsimägi, the boundary between the stage and the dirt dissolved entirely. Orkesta Mendoza opened with ‘Cumbia Volcadora’, six of them in matching suits, though nothing stayed buttoned down for long. Sergio Mendoza ran the set from the keys with an accordion slung across his chest, and on his shout of “¡Derecha! ¡Izquierda!” the whole field threw its hands right, then left, in time with him. Quetzal Guerrero sawed at the violin like an acrobat, Ozzy Acosta’s percussion kept the cumbia turning underneath, and Victor Hugo drove the band from the kit. Mendoza grew up in Ambos Nogales, the town the US-Mexico border splits in two, and the Orkesta plays what that town might sound like with the line gone: mambo, cumbia and ranchera rammed into surf guitar, psychedelia and indie rock. The Grounds kept filling as night came on, until the weekend’s largest crowd, some 8,000—packed in for Puuluup. Ramo Teder and Marko Veisson play the talharpa, a bowed lyre all but extinct outside the island of Vormsi, except they drum, bow, pluck, and brush it, feeding horsehair through loopers until a knocking, creaking rhythm rises out of a single ancient instrument. For a few numbers they brought out company: Tubli was back behind a kit, slamming real drums into a stage the pair usually run on loops and horsehair alone. In tuxedos and flat deadpan, Veisson’s voice rumbling low beneath Teder’s higher line, they sang in Estonian and a language of their own invention, stopping dead between numbers to sell the crowd straight-faced nonsense about what they’d just played. It was Veisson’s 50th, and when the field found out, thousands sang him happy birthday. He answered the only way that suited the night: throwing himself off the front to crowd-surf the field. They tried out new dance routines on the spot, saving their wildest choreography for a set that felt looser and warmer than usual. By the end, Duo Ruut were up there too: Rebane and Kivi crowding the microphones alongside Teder, Veisson, and Tubli, all five packed around the stand to see it out. Puuluup had warmed the field. OOPUS came to pound it. Mari Meentalo fed bagpipe, jaw harp and regilaul into a looper and handed the loops to Johannes Ahun’s analogue Roland synths, thousand-year-old runic song coming back out of the machines as acid house, while Aleksander Sprohgis’ lights, pinned to the beat, cracked across II Kirsimägi every time the bassline turned over and Raho Aadla danced it out at the front of the stage. OOPUS bill themselves as folk on acid and mean it to the letter: the bagpipe drone sat under a squelching acid line as though it had been waiting a millennium for exactly that, with their latest Reivlender playing as one long build. By mid-set a crowd that had spent the day watching thumb pianos and kannels was going properly, sweatily off, the oldest material on the whole bill turned into the closest thing Viljandi had to a nightclub. After midnight the festival split its mood in two. Kaevumägi turned inward for Kuula Hetke, the flute duo of Kärt Pihlap and Katariina Tirmaste, whose name translates as “listen to the moment” and whose method lives up to it: they take melodies from the home regions of their great-grandparents, Mulgimaa and Võrumaa, thread their own writing through them, and pull the whole thing apart and back together on stage. Two flutes, voice and electronics built into slow, elemental soundscapes, and beside them the visual artist Okeiko painted a video world in real time, improvising brushstrokes to match every shift in the music. The Song Festival Grounds went the other way, loud and communal, as Tuulebant+ marked ten years with a birthday set. What began as a handful of young Estonian lads deciding to play together has become a fixture of the dance floors, acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and lõõts (the Estonian button accordion) under four voices, driving the kind of brisk, folk-rooted dance music that owes a clear debt to Untsakad and the Kukerpillid before them. For the anniversary they swelled the core band out with guests borrowed from other line-ups across the weekend, the plus in the name doing real work, and sent the last of the night’s crowd home dancing. Sunday came in warm and dry and ended wringing wet. The early afternoon on I Kirsimägi got a soft landing from Tell Your Birds, an Estonian, Latvian and Italian quartet who assemble their music from old tapes and Baltic tunes, running Estonian and Latvian folk melodies and field-recorded voices through electronics into long, drifting drones. Fiddle, bowed lyre and balafon carried the tunes up front while the fourth of them worked synths and effects beneath, turning a grey start into something to wake up slowly to.  By late afternoon, the sun had pulled the crowd onto Kaevumägi for Nancy Vieira, who brought Cape Verde to Viljandi, and morna to the festival for the first time in its history. Widely seen as the heir to Cesária Évora, Vieira carries that same slow, aching island sound. Born in Guinea-Bissau to Cape Verdean parents before moving to Lisbon at 14, she embodies the exact displacement morna is written about: the voice of the person who left. Backed only by guitar, cavaquinho, light percussion, and her own cool, unhurried lead, her set folded fado, Brazilian rhythms, and West African lines into songs from her 2024 album Gente. Then came the shift: for the final numbers, she invited the crowd right up onto the stage, turning the show into a full-tilt dance through the fast, bouncing tunes of Ano Nobo. The set the weekend had quietly been saving arrived that evening, and it went to Amy Laurenson. She had barely made the festival at all, held up by flight delays, cancellations, and baggage mishandling alongside guitarist Miguel Girão, reaching Viljandi just minutes before their Saturday slot on Kaevumägi in the rain and wind. Sunday finally did her justice, placing her at a grand piano inside the Ait. There, the Shetland pianist takes fiddle tunes written for a bow and hands them to the keys as a lead voice rather than accompaniment: reels arriving with their drive intact and their phrasing completely rethought. Out of the weather, the room went dead silent and stayed that way. It was the finest hour of the four days. Fittingly, the last word went to a band from the festival’s own backyard. Angus formed in 2010 out of Viljandi and its Culture Academy, and have spent the sixteen years since turning out a warm, unhurried reggae, ska and dub sung in Estonian, their 2023 record Vibratsioon hailed by Raadio 2 as the flagship of Estonian reggae-rock. Seven of them shut the festival down from the Song Festival Grounds, joined by guest vocalist Sofia-Liis Liiv, playing out into a downpour to a soaked crowd that skanked through the mud and bouncing along to thick dub basslines and hip-hop rhymes. Before the final fade, frontman Anton Ventsel signed the weekend off with a line worth keeping: “Have a good evening, a safe journey home, and folk is forever.” A local band, on the last stage, in the wet, closing a festival their own town has built its name on. Viljandi did not have its biggest year, but it had a better one than that. The man at the hotel desk had the right instinct and the wrong month. items.body: Dau, the moniker of UK ambient musician Phil Self, is about to release his solo debut, Zed Zed. Arriving via Phantom Limb’s new sub-label imprint Spirituals, which promotes ‘high grade, emotive ambient and experimental music from emerging artists from across the world’, Zed Zed is a beautifully-crafted and intricately-woven record, utilising classical chamber orchestration and blending it with an ambient core. Self is involved in many other projects, from the UK instrumental sextet yndi halda to performing in the live band of folk-rock singer-songwriter Will Varley. Self also runs the Isolation Choir, a non-profit initiative for the elderly and the vulnerable, where musicians and non-musicians alike are invited to contribute remotely to pieced-together ensemble performances (the first video of which caught the eye of Brian Eno, who was so moved by the performance and the compassionate message behind the project that he offered his services for the second). Zed Zed features bowed guitar, reed organ, and voice, but Self also includes recordings of water bowls, falling rain, and sounds from his kitchen, which produces a warm, comfortable, and homely atmosphere, adding degrees of personality and intimacy within the familiar environment of home. The human qualities of empathy, kindness, and care are literally at the centre of the music, a point at which it can brightly shine, and it also reflects Self’s own personality, the music acting as a conduit for his inner kindness. The music unravels with patience, slowly developing and building upon itself. Perhaps most importantly, Zed Zed is free of computer processing; digital editing and computer interference is rejected. The record is entirely acoustic and proud of the fact, featuring real-time performances and nothing but acoustic instrumentation. A deep ambient heart beats within its music, which is all the more evident in the dulled harmonic resonance of its water bowl. And along with the sound of dripping water, reverberating gongs help to produce calming sensations and feelings of immense relief. With graceful movements, the music never seems to put a foot wrong. ‘Sundowning’ closes the album as an overlapping family of lean, slanting strings provide the last flares of light. Even with the sunset and its representation of ending and finality, the music’s message is one of enduring beauty, optimism, and appreciation, retaining its grace right up until its end. PSALM003: Zed Zed by Dau www.phantomlimblabel.bandcamp.com

items.body: Never The Right Time (Modern Love, April 16) is Andy Stott’s first release since 2016’s Too Many Voices. In the years since, the world has experienced seismic change, but Stott’s innovative approach is still as sharp as ever. Never The Right Time includes a host of almost-love songs. Halfway to becoming romanticized but still embedded in the thorns and false comfort of nostalgia, its pre-heated electronic slush sits well with a three a.m. haze. Andy Stott is an expert at crafting a cocktail of warm techno and fizzing mutated pop, but Never The Right Time is a record of renewal, risen spirit, and the overriding power of music as a vehicle for change. All of the tracks flow seamlessly together, and its electronic webwork creates an intimate musical encounter, emanating strong degrees of club-heat while it continues to roll forward. The humane feel to the album’s songs – softer, warmer – allows a feeling of fragility, openness, and vulnerability. The songs could snap at any moment, and some of them do. ‘Repetitive Strain’, for instance, with its rhythmic palpitations and dense melodic strobes, cuts off without warning, its lifeline severed. On the whole, Never The Right Time has an unfailing warmth at its centre, and the drums still have an energetic snap to them, despite a noticeable melancholia, which drapes itself over the record. It’s hard to move on from something of that magnitude without being pulled back into the tragedy; it can’t easily be forgotten or erased. The Coronavirus pandemic had something to do with this, of course, as Stott found himself in a state of pause. However, growth was occurring even in the stasis. The massive life changes and general turbulence of 2020 triggered a newfound purpose and an explosion of musical creativity, and Stott used it as a force for positivity, directing his flow of thoughts and taking back some semblance of control when nothing else could be controlled. The virus was an outside event which took up the mantle of dictator, changing billions of lives and inflicting suffering on millions, either directly or indirectly. Together with Alison Skidmore’s warm vocals, the record took on a different form and shape, quickly becoming more human and empathetic, even though it was electronically designed. The record’s emotional messaging ensures a ferocity that’s every bit an equal to a techno-bred, monstrous onslaught – just inhabiting a different body, with a key shift in its tone and mood. It’s slower, more thoughtful, and warmer – perhaps even more appreciative of what it’s been through – while still elevating Stott’s musicianship. Radiating melodies blur with Alison’s vocals, but some of the tracks have more of a bite to them, such as ‘Answers’, which rewinds the clock and serves up healthy slabs of bass-beef. The black belt beats are still supplied, but it’s the warmth of the record that literally shines through. Containing some innovative angles and surprising emotional hits, Never The Right Time has released at the perfect time, and it never misses a beat. www.boomkat.com

items.body: All hope abandon, ye who enter in These words in sombre color I beheld Written upon the summit of a gate Like any new Krallar title, w/d (released at the tail end of 2017), is a scary proposition I approach with trepidation. To paraphrase Dasa Drndic’s from her novel Belladonna, which addresses some of the 20th century worst human atrocities, Krallar-land is a dark and neglected territory, sunk into a cataclysmic sepulchre. Warning signs sound off from the word go with the opener Generosity Crash Test, distress signals from a post-industrial wasteland resonate, while a disembodied voice, like a malfunctioning Siri with a hangover, briefly blips into action suggesting a panoptical world slowly disintegrating. Someone has abandoned ship a long time again, forgetting to disconnect electronic circuits that still capture radio signals. Treading on a carpet of static, Krallar touches on themes of addiction and withdrawal, as a life condition possibly unrelated to substance abuse, flicking switches, turning lights off and on in a void, whilst still moving forward with a gentle degree of tolerance for distortion, even when no exit sign is clearly visible. The tension eventually eases off, with luminous loops that succeed in clearing debris from the horizon. Suddenly, I find myself floating above the abyss, becoming increasingly distant, growing smaller to the point of silence, to disappearance. I could be anywhere, it does not matter now. A becalmed sea sways once again against the walls of my skull. Cruising at high altitude, I am eventually pulled back into orbit by the gravitational pull of language. Snatches from foreign language course tapes teaching pronunciation, allude to a communication impasse. “Siri” briefly returns, now sounding more distinctly like Sylvia Plath, as if detritus from Krallar’s 2015 album Dying is an Art, came crashing in bringing a sober reminder of past trials and tribulations like an unwanted comedown. While the overall tone is still one of sombre acceptance for the inevitable reversal of fortune in life’s natural ebb and flow, for once, I was not left gasping for air with w/d. Krallar seems to have reduced the dark hue gradient to suggest, at least, the possibility of temporary solace. w/d by kr?ll?r www.krallar.bandcamp.com
